title: A Bail Application under Section 480, 482, or 483 BNSS (formerly Sections 437, 438, and 439 CrPC) is drafted to vindicate personal liberty under Article 21

content.overview: A bail application is the written request by which an accused seeks release from custody, or protection from arrest, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Section 480 BNSS corresponds to the former section 437 CrPC and is the magistrate's power in non-bailable offences. Section 482 BNSS corresponds to the former section 438 CrPC and is anticipatory bail. Section 483 BNSS corresponds to the former section 439 CrPC and is the special power of the High Court and the Court of Session. The draft must name the correct section, the court, the FIR or crime number, the custody status, the grounds, and the conditions offered. Article 21 is the liberty setting. The phrase that bail is the rule is a case-law proposition and is not restated here as a verified holding.
content.short: A Bail Application under Section 480, 482, or 483 BNSS (formerly Sections 437, 438, and 439 CrPC) is drafted to vindicate personal liberty under Article 21. It asserts the fundamental principle that "bail is the rule, jail is the exception" through testable grounds of parity, roots in society, lack of flight risk, and absence of need for custodial interrogation.
content.detailed:
Core Drafting Skeleton & Rules for Bail Applications under BNSS, 2023

1. Cause Title & Forum of Filing
   • IN THE COURT OF THE LEARNED SESSIONS JUDGE AT [Station]
   • or IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT [City]
   • Bail Application No. … of 20…
   • In connection with FIR No. … / 20… under Sections … of BNS, P.S. …
   • [Applicant / Accused Name] … Applicant vs. State (Govt. of NCT / State of …) … Respondent

2. Nature of Application & Section Heading
   • Regular Bail: Under Section 483 BNSS (Sessions/HC) or Section 480 BNSS (Magistrate).
   • Anticipatory Bail: Under Section 482 BNSS (Court of Session / High Court).
   • Default / Statutory Bail: Under Section 187(2) BNSS (formerly 167(2) CrPC) upon failure to file chargesheet within 60 or 90 days.

3. Factual Matrix & Grounds of False Implication
   • Brief narrative of the dispute, highlighting purely civil, commercial, or matrimonial genesis.
   • Clear demonstration that the applicant has been roped in falsely with omnibus, vague allegations and zero specific overt act.

4. Essential Legal Grounds for Grant of Bail
   • No custodial interrogation required: Interrogation complete, alleged weapon or articles already recovered, documents are in safe custody.
   • Doctrine of Parity: Co-accused persons having identical or higher roles have already been enlarged on regular/anticipatory bail by the Court.
   • Deep Roots in Society: Applicant has fixed permanent abode, family, dependants, and immovable properties; zero possibility of absconding or flight risk.
   • Non-tampering & Cooperation: Solemn undertaking to cooperate with investigation, appear whenever summoned, and not tamper with prosecution witnesses.
   • Clean Antecedents: Statement that applicant has no prior criminal records or convictions.
   • Statutory Protections: Non-compliance by police with notice under Section 35(3) BNSS (formerly 41A CrPC); guidelines in Arnesh Kumar and Satender Kumar Antil.
   • Proviso to Section 480(1) BNSS: Special consideration for women, children under 16, sick, or infirm persons.

5. Details of Prior Applications
   • Mandatory disclosure of whether any prior bail application was filed in this or any other court, and the outcome.

6. Prayer Clause
   • Order release of the applicant on bail in the event of arrest (anticipatory) or from judicial custody (regular), on furnishing solvent surety and personal bond.

7. Verification & Supporting Affidavit (Signed by pairokar/relative if accused is in judicial custody, or applicant personally if anticipatory).

cases.name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC (now s. 482 BNSS) is a key safeguard of Article 21; powers of High Courts and Sessions Courts are wide and should not be burdened with unwarranted conditions.
cases.relevance: Foundational Constitution Bench ruling on anticipatory bail principles.

cases.name: Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi)
cases.holding: Confirmed that protection granted under Section 438 CrPC does not invariably end upon the filing of chargesheet or framing of charges; it can normally continue till the conclusion of the trial.
cases.relevance: Duration of anticipatory bail and absence of automatic expiry.

cases.name: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
cases.holding: Laid down comprehensive nationwide category-wise bail guidelines (Categories A to D), stressing that bail must be granted without arrest where appearance notice is complied with.
cases.relevance: Standard operating bail procedure and liberty jurisprudence in trial courts.

bareActPointers: Section 480 BNSS (Bail in non-bailable offences before Magistrate)
Section 482 BNSS (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest / Anticipatory Bail)
Section 483 BNSS (Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail)
Section 479 BNSS (Maximum period for detention of undertrial prisoner)
Section 187 BNSS (Default / Statutory bail upon expiry of 60/90 days)
Section 35 BNSS (Arrest procedures and notice of appearance)
examTips: Remember the mapping: s. 437 CrPC → s. 480 BNSS; s. 438 CrPC → s. 482 BNSS; s. 439 CrPC → s. 483 BNSS; s. 436A CrPC → s. 479 BNSS.
Under Section 479 BNSS, a first-time offender (never convicted previously) is eligible for release on personal bond upon completing one-third of the maximum sentence.
Sessions Court and High Court enjoy concurrent jurisdiction for anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS.
Default bail under Section 187(2) BNSS is an indefeasible fundamental right; once 60/90 days lapse without chargesheet, the court has no discretion to refuse bail.

enhancement.definition: A bail application is the petition for release, or for a direction against arrest, under section 480, 482 or 483 BNSS, in the court that has that power.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The section follows the facts. A magistrate draft that cites the High Court's special power, or an anticipatory draft filed after arrest, is the wrong instrument.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: BNSS sections 480, 482 and 483, corresponding to CrPC sections 437, 438 and 439. Bailable offences are section 478 BNSS, formerly section 436 CrPC. Article 21 is the liberty context, not the bail section.
essentialIngredients: FIR or crime number, police station and offences
Whether the applicant is in custody or apprehends arrest
Grounds tied to the alleged role
Prayer for release or anticipatory direction
Verification and annexures: FIR, remand order, medical papers if any
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The opening must state the forum and the section. Section 480 is bail in a non-bailable offence by a court other than the High Court or Court of Session. Section 482 is a direction for bail in the event of arrest, before the Sessions Court or High Court. Section 483 is the special power of those two courts over a person in custody, and it includes the power to set aside conditions or grant bail where the magistrate has refused. The body should give the date of the FIR, the date of arrest if any, the role alleged, and the specific reason release is sought: completion of custodial purpose, parity only if a co-accused order is annexed, roots and surety, or a narrow role. The prayer must match the section. An already arrested applicant cannot be given an anticipatory prayer. Former CrPC numbers may be named in a transition sentence. They are not the operative citation after 1 July 2024.
examples: An accused in magistrate custody in a non-bailable case files under section 480, with the remand order annexed.
A person named in an FIR but not arrested files under section 482 before Sessions, seeking a direction if arrested.
A magistrate refuses bail. The next draft is section 483 before Sessions, not a second section 480 copy with a new label.

Section 483 is the Sessions or High Court power.
Do not cite old CrPC 482 as the bail section.

verification.note: Section correspondence taken from the enacted renumbering used in the existing topic and standard BNSS tables. Subsection wording and the 'bail is the rule' slogan are not treated as verified holdings.

content.study: Choose the section before writing grounds. Anticipatory bail is pre-arrest and goes to the Sessions Court or High Court under section 482. A person already in custody before a magistrate uses section 480 if that court can grant it, or section 483 before Sessions or the High Court. Do not cite CrPC 482, which was the old quashing power, as the bail section.
